about: What to Notice: guided looks at a work, one detail at a time. Written for this app from general art-history knowledge, not by the museum. Regions are fractions of the picture: x, y, width, height.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Saint Francis of Assisi has fainted, held by an angel. Caravaggio painted it in Rome around 1595, probably his first religious picture. When the Wadsworth bought it in 1943, it was the first Caravaggio in an American museum.

steps.title: The swoon
steps.text: Francis lies back with closed eyes. The story says he received the wounds of Christ on a mountain; Caravaggio shows it as a quiet collapse, not a vision in the sky.

steps.title: The wound
steps.text: His hand rests at his side, near a small tear in his robe: the wound in his side. It is easy to miss.

steps.title: The angel
steps.text: The angel is a real young man with wings, holding Francis tenderly. Caravaggio painted holy figures from ordinary models, which shocked some people.

steps.title: Light in the dark
steps.text: Far back, in the night, streaks of light glow in the sky. All the rest is darkness: only the two figures are lit, as if on a stage.

steps.title: The rough robe
steps.text: Francis’s brown habit is patched and heavy, tied with a knotted cord. Bare feet stick out at the bottom: a poor friar, painted with dignity.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.text: Caravaggio’s strong contrasts of light and dark changed European painting. This picture is one of his earliest experiments with it.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Artemisia Gentileschi, one of the most successful women painters of the 1600s, shows herself playing the lute. She painted it in Florence around 1615–18.

steps.title: Looking at us
steps.text: She turns to look straight at us while she plays, as if interrupted. Her expression is confident, even a little challenging.

steps.title: The turban
steps.text: A light turban wraps her hair. Painters liked to dress up in costume, and so did Artemisia.

steps.title: Hands on the strings
steps.text: Her left hand presses the strings on the neck of the lute, the right one plucks them below. The hands are carefully painted, as a musician’s would be.

steps.title: The lute
steps.text: Look at the carved rose in the middle of the lute and the thin lines of the strings catching the light.

steps.title: The blue dress
steps.text: The shiny blue silk, with gold embroidery, tells us she is prosperous and well dressed: a woman of standing, not a servant.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.text: Women were rarely allowed to train as painters then. Artemisia became the first woman member of the Florentine academy of art, in 1616. The Wadsworth acquired this self-portrait in 2014.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Vincent van Gogh painted this self-portrait in Paris in 1887. He painted himself many times there, partly because he couldn’t afford to pay models.

steps.title: The look
steps.text: He turns his head over his shoulder and stares at us, frowning slightly. It feels as if we had just interrupted him.

steps.title: Orange and blue
steps.text: His orange beard sits against a deep blue background. Orange and blue are opposites on the colour wheel, so each makes the other stronger. Van Gogh had learned this in Paris.

steps.title: Strokes of colour
steps.text: Look at his hair and face: short strokes of yellow, green, red and white sit side by side. Up close they are separate colours; from a distance they become skin and hair.

steps.title: The jacket
steps.text: His blue jacket is made of long, quick lines, almost like weaving.

steps.title: Bare canvas
steps.text: In the background you can see the texture of the canvas through thin paint. Van Gogh worked quickly and often on cheap supports.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.text: When he arrived in Paris in 1886, his colours were dark. Two years among the Impressionists turned them bright, and this portrait shows the change.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A valley in Jamaica, with rain on one side and sunlight on the other. Frederic Edwin Church painted it in 1867 for Elizabeth Colt of Hartford, after a trip he made to the island.

steps.title: Rain and sun
steps.text: On the left, a curtain of rain hides the sun, which glows as an orange disc. Church loved weather in motion.

steps.title: The bright gap
steps.text: In the centre, light breaks through the clouds and pours onto the valley. Your eye goes straight there.

steps.title: The tree fern
steps.text: On the right, a tall tree fern frames the view. Church studied tropical plants closely and drew them on the spot.

steps.title: The river
steps.text: A river winds through the valley, catching the light from the sky.

steps.title: Tiny details
steps.text: Look on top of the central hill: tiny trees stand against the bright sky. Church painted landscapes that reward a close look.

steps.title: Why it was made
steps.text: Church went to Jamaica in 1865 after losing two of his young children. Elizabeth Colt, a great collector and the widow of Samuel Colt, later left this painting to the Wadsworth.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Claude Monet paints in his garden at Argenteuil, near Paris, in 1873. His friend Pierre-Auguste Renoir painted him at work.

steps.title: Monet at the easel
steps.text: Monet stands in a hat with his palette and brushes, focused on his canvas. We see the painter from behind, as a friend would.

steps.title: Painting outdoors
steps.text: The light wooden easel was easy to carry outside. Painting in the open air was central to Impressionism.

steps.title: Dahlias
steps.text: The garden is full of dahlias, painted with quick touches of red, pink and white. The flowers are a blur of colour, not a botanical study.

steps.title: The fence
steps.text: A white picket fence separates Monet’s garden from the street and the new houses of the suburb behind.

steps.title: The suburb
steps.text: Behind the garden stand modern houses. Argenteuil was a growing town, a quick train ride from Paris.

steps.title: Signed
steps.text: Renoir signed at bottom left. At the time he and Monet often painted side by side, and their styles were very close.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A magnificent gallery packed with paintings from floor to ceiling. Giovanni Paolo Panini painted it in Rome in 1740 for Cardinal Silvio Valenti Gonzaga, to show off his collection.

steps.title: The cardinal
steps.text: The cardinal, in red, stands in the middle of the room, talking with visitors. He is the host of this world of art.

steps.title: Real paintings
steps.text: Many of the tiny paintings on the walls copy real works the cardinal owned. Panini painted miniatures of paintings inside his painting.

steps.title: A dream gallery
steps.text: The room itself, with its huge vault and sculpted ceiling, is imagined. No palace looked quite like this: it is a fantasy setting for a real collection.

steps.title: Connoisseurs
steps.text: On the left, men study drawings and prints, argue and point. Collecting was also a social activity.

steps.title: On the floor
steps.text: Paintings, books and drawings lie on the floor. There is so much art that it doesn’t fit on the walls.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.text: It is a portrait of a collector, and of 18th-century Rome as a capital of art. Fitting for the Wadsworth, the oldest public art museum in the United States.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Kaaterskill Falls in the Catskill Mountains of New York, seen from inside the cave behind the falls. Thomas Cole painted it in 1826.

steps.title: Inside the cave
steps.text: The dark arch of rock frames the whole scene, as if we were standing in the cave looking out.

steps.title: The waterfall
steps.text: The water drops in a white column and bursts into spray at the bottom.

steps.title: Spray and mist
steps.text: The mist is painted with soft, light strokes that glow against the dark rocks.

steps.title: Autumn colours
steps.text: Red and orange leaves show it is autumn. Cole made the colours of the American forest one of his great subjects.

steps.title: Stormy sky
steps.text: Beyond, a pink and grey sky with distant mountains. Wild nature, without a single building.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.text: Daniel Wadsworth, who founded this museum in 1842, was a friend and early patron of Cole. Cole’s wild American landscapes started the Hudson River School of painting.
